title: Case 2 of "The Inevitable Present: Integration at William & Mary"
description: Shown here is an image of Case 2 of the "'The Inevitable Present': Integration at William & Mary" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) and the Read & Relax area of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 4th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: The rejection letters received by African American applicants to William & Mary in the 1950s are strikingly similar. While some were turned away because of a late or incomplete application, most rejections included a statement like this: “The College of William & Mary is a state-supported institution of the Commonwealth of Virginia which complies with all its laws, rules and regulations. We may not enroll Negroes except as provided for under the statutes of the Commonwealth.” Letters generally closed with a referral for the applicant to Virginia State College, the present-day Virginia State University in Petersburg and a refund of the application fee. One applicant who received such a rejection letter in the summer of 1955 was Barbara Blayton, daughter of the late Alleyne Houser Blayton and Dr. J. Blaine Blayton, a prominent Williamsburg-area physician and civic leader. Eight years later, Barbara Blayton’s younger brother Oscar would become the first African American undergraduate student admitted to William & Mary. Office of the President, Davis Young Paschall Records, UA 2.15, Acc. 1982.74, Box 33, Folder 34: Negro Education, 1954-1971 hdl.handle.net/10288/17356 New Journal and Guide, 2 July 1955 The article is available through the ProQuest Historical Newspapers database at proxy.wm.edu/login?url=http://search.proquest.com/docview... Another woman rejected by William & Mary in June 1955 was Miriam Johnson Carter, since her chosen course of study, Education, was offered by Virginia State College. Mrs. Carter was on sabbatical from her teaching position in Philadelphia for the 1955-1956 school year, and wished to spend this time taking classes near her family in Gloucester, Virginia. After her initial application was denied, she exchanged letters with William & Mary administrators attempting to gain admission to a different graduate program. Her request to study at the Institute of Early American History and Culture was denied because the Institute was a research organization that did not support students. She then inquired about taking courses at the Virginia Fisheries Lab, the present-day Virginia Institute of Marine Science, but was told that, while her grades were sufficient, her coursework was not advanced enough. At the beginning of August 1955, now at her family’s home in Gloucester, Carter again requested admission to the Education program. Another exchange of correspondence between Carter, William & Mary, and this time also Richmond followed. As a result, Miriam Johnson Carter was finally accepted to study law during the 1955-1956 academic year, making her the first African American woman admitted to William & Mary during the decades-long process of desegregation. Carter’s correspondence with administrators is unique in its length and persistence. Office of the President, Davis Young Paschall Records, UA 2.15, Acc. 1982.74, Box 33, Folder 34: Negro Education, 1954-1971 hdl.handle.net/10288/17356 In 1967, Lynn Briley, Janet Brown, and Karen Ely became the first African American female undergraduate students as well as the first African American residential students at William & Mary. The three did not know one another previously nor did they know they would be roommates living together in Jefferson Hall basement. Integration at William & Mary was not simply accomplished overnight or with the admission of the first African American residential or female students, but was part of a long process of the university and its people. In 2011, the Hulon Willis Association honored the three alumnae during Homecoming festivities, which marked their 40th class reunion. In 2012, a plaque was hung in Jefferson Hall honoring Briley, Brown, and Ely. creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 3 of "The Inevitable Present: Integration at William & Mary"
description: Shown here is an image of Case 3 of the "'The Inevitable Present': Integration at William & Mary" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) and the Read & Relax area of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 4th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: In 1963, Oscar Blayton was admitted to William & Mary as the first undergraduate African American student. A local resident, Blayton is the son of the late Alleyne Houser Blayton and Dr. J. Blaine Blayton, prominent Williamsburg-area physician and civic leader, and also the younger brother of Barbara Blayton, who herself was denied admission to a William & Mary summer session in 1955. Oscar Blayton graduated from Palmer Memorial Academy in Greensboro, North Carolina and applied to William & Mary as well as Howard University. He had already been accepted at Howard when he received a call from the Dean of Admissions Robert Hunt inviting him and his parents to a meeting to discuss attending William & Mary in the fall. Blayton’s enrollment at William & Mary was another step in the decades-long process of desegregation at the university. While attending William & Mary, Blayton lived at home and commuted to campus. Newspaper articles about Blayton published in 1964 offer insight into his experiences as a student, while excerpts from a 1990 interview and other material from Swem Library’s Special Collections Research Center provide further context to his experiences at the time and in retrospect. After two years at the college, Blayton was drafted and upon completing his service in the Marines, he did not return to the university. He became a lawyer and continues to practice in the Williamsburg area. Oscar Blayton joined the Backdrop Club in his sophomore year after being approached by legendary theater professor Howard Scammon while registering for classes. “Howard initiated the conversation by asking in a typically dramatic fashion: ‘Do you play the piano?’ Dumbfounded, and having no idea why I was being asked this question, I shook my head and said ‘No’ very slowly.” Scammon went on to explain that he wanted to produce William Saroyan's “Time of Your Life” and needed to find either “a piano player that I can make look like a Negro or I have to find a Negro that I can make look like a piano player.” While Blayton got the part, they later learned that Bernard Bailey, another local African American, had just transferred to William & Mary and that, unlike Oscar Blayton, he did know how to play the piano. Blayton then found a place on campus with the Backdrop Club and in 1990 related that “over the course of a few weeks, I met and made more friends in the Backdrop Club than I had made during my entire first year at the College.” Jacqueline Filzen’s 2012 Charles Center Summer Research paper “African Americans at the College of William and Mary from 1950-1970” offers further information on this subject and provided much useful material for this exhibit. The paper can be read at hdl.handle.net/10288/17049 This essay, written by Blayton after the death of Davis Y. Paschall continues the conversation about the history of segregation and integration in Virginia and the roles of individuals during that time period. Blayton closes by stating that “[Paschall’s] record needs to be clearly understood if we are to recognize the problems in our past and prepare for a better future.” Before taking the helm as president of William & Mary, Paschall served as Virginia’s Superintendent of Public Instruction from 1957 to 1960, during Massive Resistance, a campaign to prevent integration in Virginia. Oscar Blayton was featured in this Flat Hat article during his third semester, and his comments in the fall of 1964 naturally differ from his reflections on his experience at William & Mary that he expressed later in life. While Blayton never had a direct confrontation with President Paschall, there were reported tensions surrounding Blayton’s attendance. In 1977, Milton “Bucky” Reigelman ’64, a former editor of the Flat Hat, shared in an oral history interview that Paschall “blew up, charging that we were trying to incite an issue, and would needlessly bring great wrath on the College” when it was mentioned to Paschall that the newspaper would be doing a feature on Blayton as “Student of the Week.” In the opinion of Reigelman and Blayton, Paschall was overly concerned with the reaction of conservative legislators and alumni to the beginnings of integration at William & Mary. The Flat Hat, 30 October 1964 hdl.handle.net/10288/5395 The Flat Hat student newspaper, first published in 1911, was digitized by Swem Library and is available from the W&M Digital Archive at digitalarchive.wm.edu/handle/10288/20 As his first year at William & Mary was coming to a close, the local Williamsburg newspaper planned to write a story about Oscar Blayton. Blayton was willing to be interviewed, but William & Mary president Davis Y. Paschall resisted attempts by the Virginia Gazette to get a statement from a William & Mary official and discouraged the publication of any article about Blayton. Looking back in 1990 with some distance, Blayton reflected on the article about his admission to William & Mary stating: “I would say I was more tolerated than accepted.” It was unusual for a student to have his or her own file in the records of the Office of the President like the one for Oscar Blayton reproduced here. Pomfret. Pomfret would depart William & Mary soon after Willis and Travis were admitted due to the unrelated football scandal of 1951. creator: W&M Libraries
title: Introduction to "'The Inevitable Present': Integration at William & Mary"
description: Shown here is the introduction to the "'The Inevitable Present': Integration at William & Mary" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) and the Read & Relax area of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 4th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the introductory text: “But, we are not facing history and tradition now. We are facing the inevitable present; not necessarily a crisis but a fact. Future historians will certainly have an interest in what we do with it. To the future we are on trial.” So wrote Charles P. McCurdy in his editorial published in the October 1950 issue of the Alumni Gazette about how William & Mary might handle the anticipated admission applications from African Americans students. Integration at William & Mary was not achieved simply with the acceptance of the first students of color; instead it has been a decades-long process. On June 5, 1950, the U.S. Supreme Court handed down decisions in McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents and Sweatt v. Painter, which ruled that a public institution of higher learning could not provide different treatment to students solely because of race, as doing so deprived the students of their Fourteenth Amendment right of Equal Protection. McLaurin had applied to the graduate program in education at the University of Oklahoma, while Sweatt had applied to the University of Texas School of Law. In Virginia, Gregory Swanson filed suit to gain admission to the University of Virginia's law school, which had turned him down in 1949, and with the help of the NAACP, he won in federal court and was admitted. William & Mary’s response to these events was typical of that of other universities: it admitted a small number of African American students to graduate programs, while continuing to deny them admission as undergraduates. On September 30, 1950, the College of William & Mary Board of Visitors released their statement “The Admission of Qualified Negroes to Professional and Graduate Programs,” which would eventually open William & Mary to desegregation. In this statement, the Board of Visitors determined “that the applications for admission to graduate and professional programs not offered elsewhere in the Commonwealth be referred to the Attorney General for an opinion, and that the College act in accordance with such opinion.” The headings in McCurdy’s Alumni Gazette editorial are telling: ‘unseemly as it may be’; ‘university fought and lost’; ‘freedom is expensive’; ‘equality difficult to define’; and ‘we cannot secede again.’ From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

Born to a Scottish mother and Japanese father, Matsu was an exceptional athlete who was successfully recruited from Cleveland by William & Mary to play quarterback and became captain of the football team. He also played basketball, baseball, ran track, became a member of the 13 Club and the Varsity Club, and took part in other student activities. description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of the "'The Inevitable Present': Integration at William & Mary" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) and the Read & Relax area of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 4th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: In late 1950, the Dean of the Department of Jurisprudence, Dudley W. Woodbridge reinforced the statements of the Board of Visitors and the Alumni Gazette when he told a meeting of the Norfolk and Portsmouth Bar Association that William & Mary would accept African American applicants. Edward Augustus Travis was the first African American law student at William & Mary entering in the 1951 fall semester and graduating in August 1954 with a BCL degree, making him the first African American alumnus of William & Mary. Travis, born in Reed’s Ferry, Virginia, had attended Hampton Institute and graduated from Florida A&M before applying to William & Mary. Travis passed away in Newport News in November 1960. While William & Mary had cracked open a door to integration, other battles continued throughout the nation, including in Washington, D.C. The Coordinating Committee for the Enforcement of the D.C. Anti-Discrimination Laws sent this flyer to William & Mary president Alvin Duke Chandler asking him to share the group’s boycott of department store Hecht’s with students. There is no indication in the records of the Office of the President if Chandler shared this information with students or others. Hulon Willis was the first African American student admitted to William & Mary. He began in the summer 1951 term, pursuing his masters of education. At the time of his admision, Willis was already a graduate of Virginia State College (now Virginia State University) and a teacher in the Norfolk school system. He earned his degree from William & Mary in August 1956. The William & Mary Alumni Association’s Hulon Willis Association, a constituent group founded in 1992 by and for African American alumni, was named in honor of Willis, preserving his name and place in the university’s history for the future. As a graduate student, Willis naturally had a different experience on campus than today’s undergraduate students. During the summers when he was attending classes, Willis lived on Braxton Court in a boarding house operated by Miss Gwen Skinner. When they attended football games at William & Mary, Hulon & Alyce Willis sat in the student section, not in the end zone where other African Americans were seated in the segregated stadium. When Willis was inducted into Kappa Delta Pi, an education honor society, according to Mrs. Willis another member told the group that he would be not be a part of an organization that admitted an African American. The group told this member he could leave and Willis was inducted in August 1956. As an alumnus, Willis joined the Order of the White Jacket, an Alumni Association constituent group for those who worked in campus dining halls, Colonial Williamsburg restaurants, and other dining establishments. After earning his graduate degree, Willis became an assistant professor at Virginia State University and then the director of campus police. Like all students applying to William & Mary at the time, Willis was required to include a photograph of himself with his application. In a 2005 oral history interview with Jenay Jackson ’05, Hulon Willis’ wife Alyce, who had encouraged her husband to apply to William & Mary, recounted that upon receiving his acceptance letter in March 1951, she wondered if the photograph had fallen off his application. But a few weeks later, William & Mary released a public statement, announcing that Willis was the first African American student admitted to the institution. Willis was accepted not because the institution was opening its doors to all potential African American students, but because of the case brought by Gregory Swanson against the University of Virginia in 1950 after he was denied admission to the university’s School of Law. The U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Swanson could not be barred from admission because of his race. Willis was pursuing his master’s degree specializing in physical education and since that program of study was not offered by a state-supported institution accepting African American applicants, William & Mary could not decline to admit Willis based solely on his race. The college established a procedure to confer with Attorney General J. Lindsay Almond, Jr. in Richmond on the admission of African American applicants beginning in the 1950s. William & Mary specifically wished to avoid a court case, while some, like A. W. Bohannan, who wrote to President Pomfret in May 1951 after Hulon Willis’ admission, saw forcing applicants to take the institution to court as the next step in preventing integration. William & Mary’s first non-white undergraduate student was Art Matsu, ’28. Born to a Scottish mother and Japanese father, Matsu was an exceptional athlete who was successfully recruited from Cleveland by William & Mary to play quarterback and became captain of the football team. He also played basketball, baseball, ran track, became a member of the 13 Club and the Varsity Club, and took part in other student activities. But Matsu's attendance did not open the door widely to Asian American students. William & Mary’s student body would include only a handful of Asian and Asian American students throughout the 1930s-1950s. William & Mary admitted its first African American students under President John E. Pomfret. Pomfret would depart William & Mary soon after Willis and Travis were admitted due to the unrelated football scandal of 1951. He was replaced by former admiral Alvin Duke Chandler who was new to academia. Correspondence, internal memos, and other materials relating to integration were filed by the Office of the President in the 1950s-1960s under the heading “Negro Education.” After being transferred to the University Archives, these folder titles were maintained to document the organization and practices of the office and the era. description: Shown here is a label from Case 2 of the "'The Inevitable Present': Integration at William & Mary" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) and the Read & Relax area of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 4th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the label text: Another woman rejected by William & Mary in June 1955 was Miriam Johnson Carter, since her chosen course of study, Education, was offered by Virginia State College. Mrs. Carter was on sabbatical from her teaching position in Philadelphia for the 1955-1956 school year, and wished to spend this time taking classes near her family in Gloucester, Virginia. After her initial application was denied, she exchanged letters with William & Mary administrators attempting to gain admission to a different graduate program. Her request to study at the Institute of Early American History and Culture was denied because the Institute was a research organization that did not support students. She then inquired about taking courses at the Virginia Fisheries Lab, the present-day Virginia Institute of Marine Science, but was told that, while her grades were sufficient, her coursework was not advanced enough. At the beginning of August 1955, now at her family’s home in Gloucester, Carter again requested admission to the Education program. Another exchange of correspondence between Carter, William & Mary, and this time also Richmond followed. As a result, Miriam Johnson Carter was finally accepted to study law during the 1955-1956 academic year, making her the first African American woman admitted to William & Mary during the decades-long process of desegregation. Carter’s correspondence with administrators is unique in its length and persistence. creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 3 of "The Inevitable Present: Integration at William & Mary"
description: Shown here is an image of Case 3 of the "'The Inevitable Present': Integration at William & Mary" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) and the Read & Relax area of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 4th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: In 1963, Oscar Blayton was admitted to William & Mary as the first undergraduate African American student. A local resident, Blayton is the son of the late Alleyne Houser Blayton and Dr. J. Blaine Blayton, prominent Williamsburg-area physician and civic leader, and also the younger brother of Barbara Blayton, who herself was denied admission to a William & Mary summer session in 1955. Oscar Blayton graduated from Palmer Memorial Academy in Greensboro, North Carolina and applied to William & Mary as well as Howard University. He had already been accepted at Howard when he received a call from the Dean of Admissions Robert Hunt inviting him and his parents to a meeting to discuss attending William & Mary in the fall. Blayton’s enrollment at William & Mary was another step in the decades-long process of desegregation at the university. While attending William & Mary, Blayton lived at home and commuted to campus. Newspaper articles about Blayton published in 1964 offer insight into his experiences as a student, while excerpts from a 1990 interview and other material from Swem Library’s Special Collections Research Center provide further context to his experiences at the time and in retrospect. After two years at the college, Blayton was drafted and upon completing his service in the Marines, he did not return to the university. He became a lawyer and continues to practice in the Williamsburg area. Oscar Blayton joined the Backdrop Club in his sophomore year after being approached by legendary theater professor Howard Scammon while registering for classes. “Howard initiated the conversation by asking in a typically dramatic fashion: ‘Do you play the piano?’ Dumbfounded, and having no idea why I was being asked this question, I shook my head and said ‘No’ very slowly.” Scammon went on to explain that he wanted to produce William Saroyan's “Time of Your Life” and needed to find either “a piano player that I can make look like a Negro or I have to find a Negro that I can make look like a piano player.” While Blayton got the part, they later learned that Bernard Bailey, another local African American, had just transferred to William & Mary and that, unlike Oscar Blayton, he did know how to play the piano. Blayton then found a place on campus with the Backdrop Club and in 1990 related that “over the course of a few weeks, I met and made more friends in the Backdrop Club than I had made during my entire first year at the College.” Jacqueline Filzen’s 2012 Charles Center Summer Research paper “African Americans at the College of William and Mary from 1950-1970” offers further information on this subject and provided much useful material for this exhibit. The paper can be read at hdl.handle.net/10288/17049 This essay, written by Blayton after the death of Davis Y. Paschall continues the conversation about the history of segregation and integration in Virginia and the roles of individuals during that time period. Blayton closes by stating that “[Paschall’s] record needs to be clearly understood if we are to recognize the problems in our past and prepare for a better future.” Before taking the helm as president of William & Mary, Paschall served as Virginia’s Superintendent of Public Instruction from 1957 to 1960, during Massive Resistance, a campaign to prevent integration in Virginia. Oscar Blayton was featured in this Flat Hat article during his third semester, and his comments in the fall of 1964 naturally differ from his reflections on his experience at William & Mary that he expressed later in life. While Blayton never had a direct confrontation with President Paschall, there were reported tensions surrounding Blayton’s attendance. In 1977, Milton “Bucky” Reigelman ’64, a former editor of the Flat Hat, shared in an oral history interview that Paschall “blew up, charging that we were trying to incite an issue, and would needlessly bring great wrath on the College” when it was mentioned to Paschall that the newspaper would be doing a feature on Blayton as “Student of the Week.” In the opinion of Reigelman and Blayton, Paschall was overly concerned with the reaction of conservative legislators and alumni to the beginnings of integration at William & Mary. The Flat Hat, 30 October 1964 hdl.handle.net/10288/5395 The Flat Hat student newspaper, first published in 1911, was digitized by Swem Library and is available from the W&M Digital Archive at digitalarchive.wm.edu/handle/10288/20 As his first year at William & Mary was coming to a close, the local Williamsburg newspaper planned to write a story about Oscar Blayton. Blayton was willing to be interviewed, but William & Mary president Davis Y. Paschall resisted attempts by the Virginia Gazette to get a statement from a William & Mary official and discouraged the publication of any article about Blayton. Looking back in 1990 with some distance, Blayton reflected on the article about his admission to William & Mary stating: “I would say I was more tolerated than accepted.” It was unusual for a student to have his or her own file in the records of the Office of the President like the one for Oscar Blayton reproduced here. creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 1 of Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: ‘The Only Union Lady’ Pencil sketch of Mary Ann Bowden (age 15) drawn by a Union soldier at the time of the Battle of Williamsburg. She was the daughter of Lemuel Bowden, an ardent Unionist. It bears the note: ‘Williamsburg College Hospital.’ Bowden was installed as mayor by the United States Army. The Bowden House, now known as the Armistead House is located on Duke of Gloucester Street. Bruton Parish Church Vestry Minutes, 1865 Thomas Ambler, the rector of Bruton Parish Church, refused to say the prayer for the president of the United States as printed in the Book of Common Prayer. While the church was closed, Ambler had secret prayer meetings in his house. The church reopened briefly but was closed again in 1863. This entry shows that the church was trying to gather its property in the fall of 1865 to be able to reopen. The October 1865 entry was written recto-verso on the same leaf of paper, and for display purposes the two pages have been reproduced facing each other. Diary, 1862, of Harriette Cary Diary, kept by twenty-four year old Harriette Cary during the occupation of Williamsburg. She kept the diary for three months immediately after the Battle of Williamsburg. In June of 1862, the townspeople were caring for the Confederate wounded and reading Northern newspapers. Account, 1864, of a trip by Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman The entire peninsula from Norfolk to Williamsburg was occupied by federal forces. But the area around Richmond was still held by the Confederacy. Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman traveled from Richmond to within thirteen miles of Williamsburg to retrieve some of her belongings sent out of the occupied town by her mother. She also was able to warn Confederate troops that the Union guard at Williamsburg had been doubled and not to attack. Letters, 1862, of Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman married Doctor Charles Coleman during the Civil War. Although she was absent from Williamsburg during part of the occupation, she wrote these letters concerning the treatment of wounded Confederate prisoners in Williamsburg to Col. Campbell, a Union army officer. Busteed Order Following the Confederate Raid on Williamsburg, 29 March 1863 The raid on Williamsburg by Confederate troops, 29 March 1863, resulted in an order by Brigadier-General Richard Busteed, stating that the “attack was aided, if not planned, by citizens of Williamsburg and carried to a successful end by them . . .” and giving the punishment for the citizens. The order was countermanded the next day by Major-General John A. Dix. Lithograph, “Williamsburg Female Academy. Virginia.” Drawn by W. F. Grabau Printed by P. S. Dubal’s Steam Lith. Press, Philadelphia The Williamsburg Female Academy was incorporated in 1839 by the Virginia General Assembly. It stood where the colonial capitol does now and was used as a barrack for federal soldiers during the Union occupation of Williamsburg. Robert A. Saunders, Williamsburg, Va. to Lucy Burwell Saunders, Hanover, Va., 12 September 1862 Saunders had been president of the College of William & Mary from 1847-1848. He wrote to his wife, who had fled Williamsburg, about the excessive heat and sent her word from their slaves. John Adams Dix to Henry A. Wise, 28 April 1863 Continued harassment by Confederate troops led Union Major-General John Adams Dix to write Confederate General Henry A. Wise that, if the attacks did not stop, he would release the patients of the Eastern Lunatic Asylum (now Eastern State Hospital) onto the streets of Richmond. Minié Balls and Cannon Ball, circa 1862 The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation field crew and William & Mary field school students excavated this Civil War era ammunition in the historic campus. The cannon ball was unearthed in the Wren Yard during excavations led by Steve Archer from 2005-2007. Mark Kostro led the 2011 Brafferton dig that uncovered the Minié balls exhibited here. Sally M. Galt, Williamsburg, Va. to Col. West, 3 February, 1864 The policy of the Union army was that all citizens in an occupied territory should either take the Oath of Allegiance to the United States Government or leave the territory. Sally M. Galt wrote to protest the policy and to plead to be allowed to stay. She was permitted to remain in town. Bruton Parish Church Vestry Minutes, 1865 Thomas Ambler, the rector of Bruton Parish Church, refused to say the prayer for the president of the United States as printed in the Book of Common Prayer. While the church was closed, Ambler had secret prayer meetings in his house. The church reopened briefly but was closed again in 1863. This entry shows that the church was trying to gather its property in the fall of 1865 to be able to reopen. She kept the diary for three months immediately after the Battle of Williamsburg. In June of 1862, the townspeople were caring for the Confederate wounded and reading Northern newspapers. Account, 1864, of a trip by Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman The entire peninsula from Norfolk to Williamsburg was occupied by federal forces. But the area around Richmond was still held by the Confederacy. Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman traveled from Richmond to within thirteen miles of Williamsburg to retrieve some of her belongings sent out of the occupied town by her mother. Campbell, a Union army officer. Saunders, Williamsburg, Va. to Lucy Burwell Saunders, Hanover, Va., 12 September 1862 Saunders had been president of the College of William & Mary from 1847-1848. Wise, 28 April 1863 Continued harassment by Confederate troops led Union Major-General John Adams Dix to write Confederate General Henry A. Wise that, if the attacks did not stop, he would release the patients of the Eastern Lunatic Asylum (now Eastern State Hospital) onto the streets of Richmond. title: Case 2 of Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is an image of Case 2 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Edward R. Yoder, Freedman’s Store, Yorktown, Va. to E. J. Ransom, 25 October 1864 Yoder, possibly a Quaker teacher, described a school in Yorktown, Va. for contraband (freed blacks). He mentioned helping to raise a bell into the school house that once belonged to a Yorktown church. This may have been Grace Episcopal Church whose bell was taken to Philadelphia and later returned to the congregation. Slabtown: the African-American Presence at Yorktown As soon as Yorktown (which became known as Fort Yorktown) was abandoned by Confederate forces on May 4, 1862 and occupied by Federal troops, slaves began coming into the Union lines. Although the Emancipation Proclamation, which took effect in January of 1863, did not free slaves in occupied areas such as Yorktown, blacks, referred to as contraband of war or simply contrabands, continued to flock there. In the fall of 1863, United States Colored Troops (U. S. C. T.) arrived. After Isaac Wister took command, he ordered quarters for blacks built three-quarters of a mile from Fort Yorktown. Three communities were set up: Slabtown, Acretown (now Lackey) and Slab Richmond at Gloucester Point. Shiloh Baptist Church in Lackey was founded by contrabands in 1863 and is still active today. The Quakers (Friends Freedmen Relief Association) sent supplies, tools and teachers. They also opened stores. The National Cemetery in Yorktown where the remains of U.S.C.T. soldiers are interred, is located near Slabtown. The National Park Service maintains a permanent exhibit relating to the contraband settlement in a building near the cemetery. Grace Episcopal Church Grace Episcopal Church was built in 1697 and burned in 1814. Rebuilt in 1848, it suffered damage during the Civil War. The church with the original marl walls still stands in Yorktown today. The church bell (1725) was removed, and perhaps placed in a schoolhouse where contrabands were taught. It later made its way to Philadelphia, was recast in 1882, and then returned to the church. Yorktown Artifacts Eagle breastplate, eagle uniform button and shoulder scales (a type of epaulet), all found at Yorktown. The breastplate was supposed to cover a soldier’s heart and was worn on the strap of an ammunition box that would cover the chest. The eagle insignia was indicative of the style issued to Union forces. Cavalier (Newspaper), 12 May 1863 Newspaper published by Union troops first at Williamsburg and later at Yorktown during the occupation of the historic triangle. It was printed on the press of the Weekly Gazette and Eastern Virginia Advertiser Weekly Review. The letter of John A. Dix to Henry A. Wise was not only printed in the Cavalier, but also received wide circulation in Northern papers. Business is Booming in Yorktown The federal occupation of the port town led to small businesses springing up to serve the troops. Advertisements were published in the Cavalier, a paper printed by the troops. John Jacob Astor Telegram, 4 May 1862 John Jacob Astor served as aide-de-camp to Gen. George McClellan. Immensely wealthy, he moved to England after the war. In this telegram from Yorktown, he signaled that the rebel army had evacuated Yorktown, leaving eighty cannons behind. This evacuation would pave the way for the occupation of the town, made famous by Cornwallis’s surrender in 1781. Aerial View of Jamestown, 1998 While there was no engagement at Jamestown, it was considered a strategic defense point on the James River and, after Confederate forces abandoned it, it was occupied for the remainder of the war by Union troops. But for a brief time, no military presence was there and in late summer or early autumn of 1862, the Ambler House at Jamestown was burned by former slaves. The ruins are still visible today. Murder at Jamestown, October 1862 Jacob Morton Shriver, the uncle of Mrs. William Allen (wife of the owner of Jamestown Island) and two blacks, Littleton (slave) and Gilbert Wooten (free black) went to Jamestown along with Joseph A. Graves and his nephew George Graves (child). Seven armed slaves (formerly owned by Allen) first captured Wooten and later the rest of Wooten’s party. A crowd of about 100 blacks gathered. Joseph Graves, George Graves, Shriver, and Wooten were shot. Wooten, though shot three times, escaped, but the others were killed. title: Intro to "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle"
description: Shown here is the introductory poster of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the intro text: The Historic Triangle is a term that was used as early as the 1930s to denote the three towns which have become tourist attractions: Jamestown, site of the first permanent English settlement in North America, Williamsburg, the Revolutionary War capital of Virginia, and Yorktown where the American Revolution ended. There are two kinds of military occupation: the kind employed during a war and the kind implemented once the surrender treaty ending a broad conflict has been signed. And, psychologically, they must be different. The majority of the white people of Williamsburg, Yorktown and Jamestown hoped that a Confederate victory would soon end the war and they wanted to support that cause. Most blacks also were hoping that the war would soon be over and, increasingly, must have hoped that they would gain freedom - and during the war period many did. It was clear that the majority of the white Williamsburg population did aid the Confederates as much as they could and this meant that the Federals had to be ever alert. But much of the Historic Triangle population’s time was occupied with just gathering together the necessities of life and worrying about members of their families, who were elsewhere. Although there were isolated incidents of arrests and bad feelings, the occupation of the Historic Triangle was neither cruel nor oppressive. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

title: Case 2 of Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is an image of Case 2 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Edward R. Yoder, Freedman’s Store, Yorktown, Va. to E. J. Ransom, 25 October 1864 Yoder, possibly a Quaker teacher, described a school in Yorktown, Va. for contraband (freed blacks). He mentioned helping to raise a bell into the school house that once belonged to a Yorktown church. This may have been Grace Episcopal Church whose bell was taken to Philadelphia and later returned to the congregation. Slabtown: the African-American Presence at Yorktown As soon as Yorktown (which became known as Fort Yorktown) was abandoned by Confederate forces on May 4, 1862 and occupied by Federal troops, slaves began coming into the Union lines. Although the Emancipation Proclamation, which took effect in January of 1863, did not free slaves in occupied areas such as Yorktown, blacks, referred to as contraband of war or simply contrabands, continued to flock there. In the fall of 1863, United States Colored Troops (U. S. C. T.) arrived. After Isaac Wister took command, he ordered quarters for blacks built three-quarters of a mile from Fort Yorktown. Three communities were set up: Slabtown, Acretown (now Lackey) and Slab Richmond at Gloucester Point. Shiloh Baptist Church in Lackey was founded by contrabands in 1863 and is still active today. The Quakers (Friends Freedmen Relief Association) sent supplies, tools and teachers. They also opened stores. The National Cemetery in Yorktown where the remains of U.S.C.T. soldiers are interred, is located near Slabtown. The National Park Service maintains a permanent exhibit relating to the contraband settlement in a building near the cemetery. Grace Episcopal Church Grace Episcopal Church was built in 1697 and burned in 1814. Rebuilt in 1848, it suffered damage during the Civil War. The church with the original marl walls still stands in Yorktown today. The church bell (1725) was removed, and perhaps placed in a schoolhouse where contrabands were taught. It later made its way to Philadelphia, was recast in 1882, and then returned to the church. Yorktown Artifacts Eagle breastplate, eagle uniform button and shoulder scales (a type of epaulet), all found at Yorktown. The breastplate was supposed to cover a soldier’s heart and was worn on the strap of an ammunition box that would cover the chest. The eagle insignia was indicative of the style issued to Union forces. Cavalier (Newspaper), 12 May 1863 Newspaper published by Union troops first at Williamsburg and later at Yorktown during the occupation of the historic triangle. It was printed on the press of the Weekly Gazette and Eastern Virginia Advertiser Weekly Review. The letter of John A. Dix to Henry A. Wise was not only printed in the Cavalier, but also received wide circulation in Northern papers. Business is Booming in Yorktown The federal occupation of the port town led to small businesses springing up to serve the troops. Advertisements were published in the Cavalier, a paper printed by the troops. John Jacob Astor Telegram, 4 May 1862 John Jacob Astor served as aide-de-camp to Gen. George McClellan. Immensely wealthy, he moved to England after the war. In this telegram from Yorktown, he signaled that the rebel army had evacuated Yorktown, leaving eighty cannons behind. This evacuation would pave the way for the occupation of the town, made famous by Cornwallis’s surrender in 1781. Aerial View of Jamestown, 1998 While there was no engagement at Jamestown, it was considered a strategic defense point on the James River and, after Confederate forces abandoned it, it was occupied for the remainder of the war by Union troops. But for a brief time, no military presence was there and in late summer or early autumn of 1862, the Ambler House at Jamestown was burned by former slaves. The ruins are still visible today. Murder at Jamestown, October 1862 Jacob Morton Shriver, the uncle of Mrs. William Allen (wife of the owner of Jamestown Island) and two blacks, Littleton (slave) and Gilbert Wooten (free black) went to Jamestown along with Joseph A. Graves and his nephew George Graves (child). Seven armed slaves (formerly owned by Allen) first captured Wooten and later the rest of Wooten’s party. A crowd of about 100 blacks gathered. Joseph Graves, George Graves, Shriver, and Wooten were shot. Wooten, though shot three times, escaped, but the others were killed. Colored Cavalry 1st New York Mounted Rifles 85th Pennsylvania Infantry 76th Pennsylvania Infantry 100th Pennsylvania Infantry 16th New York Heavy Artillery 20th New York Cavalry From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. George McClellan. Immensely wealthy, he moved to England after the war. In this telegram from Yorktown, he signaled that the rebel army had evacuated Yorktown, leaving eighty cannons behind. This evacuation would pave the way for the occupation of the town, made famous by Cornwallis’s surrender in 1781. title: Label from Case 2 of the Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is a label from Case 2 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the label text: Slabtown: the African-American Presence at Yorktown As soon as Yorktown (which became known as Fort Yorktown) was abandoned by Confederate forces on May 4, 1862 and occupied by Federal troops, slaves began coming into the Union lines. Although the Emancipation Proclamation, which took effect in January of 1863, did not free slaves in occupied areas such as Yorktown, blacks, referred to as contraband of war or simply contrabands, continued to flock there. In the fall of 1863, United States Colored Troops (U. S. C. T.) arrived. After Isaac Wister took command, he ordered quarters for blacks built three-quarters of a mile from Fort Yorktown. Three communities were set up: Slabtown, Acretown (now Lackey) and Slab Richmond at Gloucester Point. Shiloh Baptist Church in Lackey was founded by contrabands in 1863 and is still active today. The Quakers (Friends Freedmen Relief Association) sent supplies, tools and teachers. They also opened stores. The National Cemetery in Yorktown where the remains of U.S.C.T. soldiers are interred, is located near Slabtown. The National Park Service maintains a permanent exhibit relating to the contraband settlement in a building near the cemetery. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

Graves and his nephew George Graves (child). Seven armed slaves (formerly owned by Allen) first captured Wooten and later the rest of Wooten’s party. A crowd of about 100 blacks gathered. Joseph Graves, George Graves, Shriver, and Wooten were shot. Wooten, though shot three times, escaped, but the others were killed. But for a brief time, no military presence was there and in late summer or early autumn of 1862, the Ambler House at Jamestown was burned by former slaves. The ruins are still visible today. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

These illnesses spread more quickly with the migration of people during the war. The occurrence of diseases also likely increased due to other war-related factors like malnutrition. The two letters in this case from Ann Maury to her niece Nan and from Nannie Watkins to her husband show the impact of childhood illness. The reference to “[w]hooping cough” is matter of fact, probably because it was a common childhood illness at the time; while on the other hand, little Charley’s death from fever was unexpected and his mother’s letter indicates a commitment to her Christian faith in dealing with her sudden loss. title: Intro Label from Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War
description: Shown here is the introductory label to Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War, an Exhibit located in the Special Collections Research Center Lobby in Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from April 17th 2013 to October 16th 2013 The following is a transcription of the intro label's text: At the beginning of the Civil War, 14 million children lived in the United States, making up more than forty percent of the country’s population. Their voices and experiences are therefore an indispensable part of any holistic understanding of life on the home front. Through primary source materials like diaries, letters, photographs, books, and artifacts Blockades, Books, and Bassinets illustrates the lives of children of various ages, stages, and locations during this period. From the mundane to the unique challenges of war, these are their stories… From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 1 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War
description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War, an Exhibit located in the Special Collections Research Center Lobby in Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from April 17th 2013 to October 16th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Play and Mischief Even during the war, children enjoyed playing: boys likely played soldiers, and girls enjoyed dolls and dress up games (fans & jewelry included, and possibly not allowed). In addition to playing, children (shockingly) misbehaved. Two such examples: Willie who decided to stay out too late and got into trouble and Charley, who according to his mother was “very bad.” Reading (and Doodling) Reading was an important skill (although many children remained illiterate) and once acquired, older children may have continued to learn about life, customs, and current events through the written word, specifically almanacs and newspapers. A very popular book series for children and young adults was “Peter Parley,” written primarily by Samuel and Charles Goodrich. Examples of these children’s books are provided throughout this case. And like many of us, the children back then may very well have doodled in their own, or their parents’ books. Learning Learning, whether at home or in school, was important for children. From reading to history to music to ciphering, learning about manners and cultivating friendships as well as assisting with younger siblings and simply using one’s imagination, were all parts of this process. Like today, childhood friendships could sometimes be fraught with drama. Sarah “Lizzie” Ladd did not share what offense her friend Nell may have been guilty of, just simply her displeasure. Siblings (surprisingly) did not always get along. In this letter, his father instructs young Charley to mind his mother and not make his sister cry. School Different types of schools, including boarding and subscription schools, existed during the Civil War. The tuition usually funded the schoolmaster’s salary. Levels of rigor varied as did the quality of the instructional materials. Textbooks at that time were called “primers.” As the war continued, the Confederacy sought to provide its own primers. The cover of one of those depicts the Sir Christopher Wren Building at the College of William & Mary. Two schools are presented in this case: New England’s Willis School, attended by Lizzie Ladd and Williamsburg’s Galt School. A New Normal While children still played, misbehaved, learned, and made friends, they also faced separation from family, hunger, and other challenges associated with the war. In this exchange of letters between Charley and his father Nathaniel, the attempts of parent and child to stay connected evoke emotions that transcend time. Clothed and Fed Picking lint for dressing wounds, knitting socks, and other efforts to assist soldiers near and far became everyday occurrences at home. Efforts to keep children clothed and shoed depended greatly upon location and resources. A tale of contrasts, even from early in the war, is depicted by these two accounts: a letter from Ann Maury (Union) and the diary of Charles Campbell (Confederate). In the South, especially, inflation was rampant and by war’s end, food and cloth were extremely expensive and often scarce; it likely took much time, money, and pluck to fill this market bag even with basic supplies. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

While the Emancipation Proclamation freed the slaves in the states in rebellion effective January 1, 1863, it was disregarded by the Confederate states, which considered themselves part of a sovereign nation. This bill of sale shows that African American children continued to be enslaved in the fall of 1863. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

Many boys, typically between the ages of nine and fifteen, assisted with the war efforts in their own backyards or served with Union and Confederate brigades in various capacities. They beat the drums of war, but also filled canteens, assisted with horses, and tended to the wounded. creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 3 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War
description: Shown here is an image of Case 3 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War, an Exhibit located in the Special Collections Research Center Lobby in Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from April 17th 2013 to October 16th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Power of Memory The Civil War impressed indelible images and memories upon those who lived through it. Some women and children, like Anna Partin and Fanny Ribble, experienced the war in their own communities. Written well after the Civil War ended, these “Lost Cause” memoirs still provide glimpses of life during evacuation, occupation, and battle, even if softened or altered by time. Enslaved Children Approximately one million children were enslaved at the beginning of the war in 1861. While the Emancipation Proclamation freed the slaves in the states in rebellion effective January 1, 1863, it was disregarded by the Confederate states, which considered themselves part of a sovereign nation. This bill of sale shows that African American children continued to be enslaved in the fall of 1863. Drummer Boys When Americans reflect upon children during the Civil War, the image of young drummer boys often comes to mind. Many boys, typically between the ages of nine and fifteen, assisted with the war efforts in their own backyards or served with Union and Confederate brigades in various capacities. They beat the drums of war, but also filled canteens, assisted with horses, and tended to the wounded. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 1 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War
description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War, an Exhibit located in the Special Collections Research Center Lobby in Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from April 17th 2013 to October 16th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Play and Mischief Even during the war, children enjoyed playing: boys likely played soldiers, and girls enjoyed dolls and dress up games (fans & jewelry included, and possibly not allowed). In addition to playing, children (shockingly) misbehaved. Two such examples: Willie who decided to stay out too late and got into trouble and Charley, who according to his mother was “very bad.” Reading (and Doodling) Reading was an important skill (although many children remained illiterate) and once acquired, older children may have continued to learn about life, customs, and current events through the written word, specifically almanacs and newspapers. A very popular book series for children and young adults was “Peter Parley,” written primarily by Samuel and Charles Goodrich. Examples of these children’s books are provided throughout this case. And like many of us, the children back then may very well have doodled in their own, or their parents’ books. Learning Learning, whether at home or in school, was important for children. From reading to history to music to ciphering, learning about manners and cultivating friendships as well as assisting with younger siblings and simply using one’s imagination, were all parts of this process. Like today, childhood friendships could sometimes be fraught with drama. Sarah “Lizzie” Ladd did not share what offense her friend Nell may have been guilty of, just simply her displeasure. Siblings (surprisingly) did not always get along. In this letter, his father instructs young Charley to mind his mother and not make his sister cry. School Different types of schools, including boarding and subscription schools, existed during the Civil War. The tuition usually funded the schoolmaster’s salary. Levels of rigor varied as did the quality of the instructional materials. Textbooks at that time were called “primers.” As the war continued, the Confederacy sought to provide its own primers. The cover of one of those depicts the Sir Christopher Wren Building at the College of William & Mary. Two schools are presented in this case: New England’s Willis School, attended by Lizzie Ladd and Williamsburg’s Galt School. A New Normal While children still played, misbehaved, learned, and made friends, they also faced separation from family, hunger, and other challenges associated with the war. In this exchange of letters between Charley and his father Nathaniel, the attempts of parent and child to stay connected evoke emotions that transcend time. Clothed and Fed Picking lint for dressing wounds, knitting socks, and other efforts to assist soldiers near and far became everyday occurrences at home. Efforts to keep children clothed and shoed depended greatly upon location and resources. A tale of contrasts, even from early in the war, is depicted by these two accounts: a letter from Ann Maury (Union) and the diary of Charles Campbell (Confederate). In the South, especially, inflation was rampant and by war’s end, food and cloth were extremely expensive and often scarce; it likely took much time, money, and pluck to fill this market bag even with basic supplies. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

title: Adam Empie Biography from Presidents of the College of William & Mary Exhibit, April 2013
description: Shown here is the Biography of Adam Empie from the Presidents of the College of William & Mary exhibit series located in the Flat case near the Brown Board Room and Library Administration on the 3rd Floor of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary. This exhibit is part of a continuing series about the presidents of the College of William & Mary. It provides a history of the College as seen through the eyes of its presidents. This fourth installment details the administration of president Adam Empie (1827-1836), and will be on display from April 18th 2013 to October 17 2013. The following is a transcription of the label text: After the sudden death of William Wilmer, the board of visitors decided to install Rev. Adam Empie, a former chaplain at the United States Military Academy, as the twelfth president of William & Mary. While president, Empie taught moral philosophy and was also rector of Bruton Parish Church. During the first few years of his tenure, the college suffered from a high faculty turnover that was later remedied by the additions of Nathaniel Beverley Tucker as professor of law and William Barton Rogers as professor of natural philosophy and chemistry. When a devastating cholera epidemic hit Williamsburg in 1832, it caused an already declining enrollment to sink from fifty-three in 1831 to a dozen or so in 1833. In order to attract students, the board of visitors offered certificates to those who performed well in one or more classes. More importantly, the teaching of ancient languages was remodeled into a classics department, as found in New England schools. Due to these efforts, enrollment slowly increased, and by the end of the 1830s, it rose to an all-time high of 140. But despite this success, the college struggled with large deficits, unpaid salaries, deteriorating buildings, and dwindling landholdings and Empie resigned the presidency in 1836 to become rector of St. James Church in Richmond, Virginia. For more information about Rev. Adam Empie, see scdb.swem.wm.edu/wiki/index.php/Adam_Empie From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

title: CHIN180 Course Description from "The Brush Dances and the Ink Sings"
description: Shown here is a label from "The Brush Dances and the Ink Sings", an exhibit located in the Third Floor Rotunda Gallery and in the lobby of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary from August 24 2013 to November 24 2013. The following is a transcription of the label text: CHIN 180: Chinese Calligraphy and Painting: Aesthetics and Practice Instructor: Philip Jun Fang Teaching Assistants: Qinao Wang, Zhiyao Lu This course on the art and practice of Chinese calligraphy and painting consists of an introduction to the history, principle and aesthetic values of Chinese characters and calligraphy and offers hands-on experience on brush composition. It also covers the connections between calligraphy, painting, poetry and philosophical thoughts, namely Taoism (yin and yang), Confucianism, and Buddhism. Students are required to finish five projects over the course of the semester, including a bamboo painting, an orchid painting, calligraphy of Chinese proverbs and poetry, and a final project that combines calligraphy and painting. For more information, please visit: wmcalligraphy.wix.com/wmcalligraphy Or contact: Philip Jun Fang, jfang01@wm.edu Qinao Wang, qwang02@email.wm.edu Shu Xuan, sxuan@wm.edu From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

creator: W&M Libraries
title: Label from "The Brush Dances and the Ink Sings"
description: Shown here is a label from "The Brush Dances and the Ink Sings", an exhibit located in the Third Floor Rotunda Gallery and in the lobby of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary from August 24 2013 to November 24 2013. The following is a transcription of the label text: How to Appreciate Calligraphy Aesthetic standards of calligraphy are rooted in the cultural and philosophical tenets of a people. In China, the major influences have been Taoism, Confucianism, and Buddhism. However, ancient Chinese artists did not explain their aesthetic principles with precise definitions the way ancient Greek scholars did. Instead, they used metaphors to expound their aesthetic ideas. For example, Chinese calligraphers compare a good stroke to “chiseling marks into sand.” Imagine you hold a chisel vertically and draw a line in the sand, the point of the chisel cuts deep into the sand while its sides push the sand aside to make a mark that contains a clear-cut center. If you produce a good center-tip stroke, the point of the brush tip “cuts” at the center of the stroke just as the point of a chisel does in sand. You feel that the center of the stroke is hard and muscular while the surface is a bit gentler yet at the same time very tough. The center of every stroke is distinct while its outline is irregular. But the irregularity is not deliberately designed. It comes into being “by itself.” In practice, one can approach calligraphy from its basic elements: the stroke and the structure. To produce a good stroke, one must learn to control the brush and move it steadily, which of course requires practice. Though the brush may sometimes move a little faster or slower, the change of speed should also be steady. A stroke produced by a well-controlled brush looks full, robust and yet supple. On the other hand, a poorly controlled brush produces weak and insipid strokes. Following are eight basic brushstrokes: The key to a good structure is balance. Just as a scholar said, “Although our ancient masters doubtless had no knowledge of mechanics, most of their characters succeed in obeying its laws! The center of gravity, for instance, is always rightly placed.” The center of gravity must fall on a base. Otherwise, the character will totter and collapse. It is widely recognized that a good composition contains good balance, or Ping Heng. However, without contrast, the effect would be too well-balanced and would result in dullness. The kind of balance used in Chinese art is an asymmetrical one. It is not 8 = 8, but rather, 8 = 5+2+1 or 8 = 4+3+1. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

description: Picture depicts the Wren Chapel of the Sir Christopher Wren Building on the Historic Campus of the College of William & Mary. As with the other buildings on Historic Campus, the Wren Building was restored by the Colonial Williamsburg project in the 1920s—1930s. The chapel's appearance is based on designs by Wren but shares very little materially with its pre-restoration renditions. The Wren Cross, which was donated by Bruton Parish and was the subject of controversy following its removal from the altar in 2006, is visible in its display case on the left.

description: When Charles M. Robinson designed the dormitories of Old Campus at the College of William & Mary, he connected each building with an arcaded pathway he dubbed "cloisters". The cloister depicted here connects Barrett Hall (right) with Chandler Hall. McGlothin-Street Hall, an academic hall along the Sunken Garden, is visible in the background in the center-left.
